name: bluewater-shorts-13-22
lines: Three years from now, their water heater quits at midnight.
Whose number is on it?
You put it in. You did it right. They were happy.
But three years is a long time. They don't remember your name.
So they grab a phone and search. And now you're one of ten strangers.
Here's the fix. Put a sticker on everything you install or service.
Your name. Your number. The date you were there.
On the tank. Inside the panel door. On the furnace.
It costs almost nothing. And it sits right where the problem happens.
You already won this customer once. Don't make yourself win them twice.
You just spent three days on that street.
And nobody there knows your name.
Think about it. The neighbours watched your truck pull up. They heard the work. They saw how it turned out.
Same houses. Same age. Same problems coming.
And then you packed up and drove away.
Next time, do two things before you leave.
Put a small sign in the yard while you work. Ask your customer first.
Then leave a note at the five closest doors. We just finished next door. If you ever need us, here's our number.
No pitch. Just hello.
You already paid to get to that street. Don't leave it with one job.
That two hundred dollar job you did yesterday?
It wasn't worth two hundred dollars.
Say that customer calls you once a year. And say they stay eight years. That's sixteen hundred.
Now say they tell one neighbour. Thirty two hundred.
Same customer. Same first job.
Here's why it matters. If you think a customer is worth two hundred, paying fifty to get one feels expensive.
If you know they're worth thirty two hundred, it's the best deal you'll make all year.
That's sales, not profit. But it changes the math.
So tonight, pick three old customers. Add up everything they ever paid you.
That's what a customer is really worth. Now you know what you can afford to win one.
Your truck is a billboard.
And right now, nobody can read it.
Here's the test. The car behind you at a red light gets a few seconds.
What do they see? A logo. A slogan. Six services in tiny letters. A website. Two phone numbers.
Too much. So they read none of it.
Strip it back to three things.
What you do, in two words. Big.
Your name.
And one phone number. Huge.
Go stand across the street. If you can't read it in three seconds, neither can they.
Your truck's out there all day anyway. Make it say something.
Somebody searched plumber salary today.
And you may have paid for that click.
Here's how. You tell Google, show my ad to people looking for a plumber.
But Google can also show it on searches it thinks are related. Plumber jobs. Plumbing school. How to fix it yourself.
Those people aren't hiring anybody. But a click is a click, and you get the bill.
The fix takes ten minutes. Open your ad account and find the search terms report.
It shows real searches that set off your ad.
Every one that makes no sense, add it as a negative keyword. That tells Google, not for this one.
Check it once a month. It might be the cheapest fix your ads ever get.
You just got a one star review.
Don't type anything yet.
Because your reply isn't for the person who wrote it. It's for the next customer who reads it.
And they're deciding one thing. Is this a business that argues?
So what would you do? Fight back? Ignore it?
Try this instead. Three sentences.
One. Thank them, and say you're sorry it went that way.
Two. Say one true thing about how you normally work.
Three. Give a name and a number, so they can reach you directly.
Then stop. No excuses. No blame. And never offer anything to take it down.
A calm reply under a bad review can say more about you than ten good ones.
You sent a quote. It was one number on a page.
So was the other guy's.
Now picture your customer at the kitchen table with both. Two numbers. Nothing else to go on.
Which one do they pick? Usually, the lower one. You gave them nothing else to compare.
So add three lines to every quote.
What's included. Spell it out, even the obvious parts.
When you can start, and how long it takes.
And what happens if something goes wrong after you leave.
Now they're not comparing two prices. They're comparing a number and a plan.
You don't have to be cheaper. You have to be clearer.
Your business has three different names.
You just haven't noticed.
On your truck, it's the short one. On Google, it's the long legal one with Limited on the end. On your invoice, it's the name you used ten years ago.
Now someone gets your name from a neighbour and looks you up.
Different name. An old phone number. Is that even the same company?
They're not going to investigate. They'll call somebody else.
So take twenty minutes. Write down one name, one phone number, one address.
Then make every place match it exactly. Google. Website. Truck. Invoice. Facebook.
Same name everywhere. It's boring. And it's how people find you twice.
When was the last time you called your own business?
Do it today. From a different phone. And just listen.
How many rings? Who picks up? And what's the first thing they say?
If it's just hello, your customer isn't sure they got the right number. Is this a business, or somebody's kitchen?
Here's a better first four seconds.
Your company name. Your first name. How can I help?
That's it. Now they know they're in the right place, and they're talking to a real person.
Write it on a card. Tape it by the phone. Everyone who answers says the same thing.
You spend real money to make that phone ring. Make the first four seconds count.
Quality work. Fair prices. Family owned.
You just described every business in your town. Including the bad ones.
Nobody says, we do sloppy work at unfair prices. So those words tell your customer nothing.
Here's the fix. Swap every vague word for something they can check.
Not, we're reliable. Say, we call thirty minutes before we arrive.
Not, quality work. Say, two year warranty, in writing.
Not, we respect your home. Say, boot covers on, and we vacuum before we leave.
Only say what you really do. Then do it every time.
Specific beats nice.
